Grade 5 · Unit 5.1

Matter, Mixtures, and Changes

What is stuff made of, and how can we tell if it changed?

  • 2 Solids, liquids, and gases act differently

Concept 1

Matter is made of tiny particles

All matter is made of particles too small to see.

Analogy

LEGO bricks from far away

a LEGO wall, then a zoomed-out view.

“From far away it looks smooth. Up close it is made of pieces.”

Diagram

Particle boxes

solid particles close together, liquid particles sliding, gas particles far apart.

“Particles in a solid are close. Particles in a liquid can slide. Particles in a gas spread out.”

Try it

Air takes space

a zip bag being blown up and sealed.

“Blow air into a bag. Seal it. Press it. The air takes space.”

Data

Air has mass

two balloons on a straw balance, one inflated.

“The inflated balloon tips down a little. If it does not, try a pumped-up ball and a flat ball on a kitchen scale. Air is matter.”

Concept 2

Solids, liquids, and gases act differently

The state of matter depends on how particles move and stay together.

Diagram

Three cups

ice cube, water, and water vapor (the gas you cannot see).

“Ice keeps its shape. Water takes the cup’s shape. Water vapor, an invisible gas, spreads out. The white cloud over a kettle is tiny droplets.”

Try it

Safe warming

ice cube in a cup, then water. Adult may help with warm water.

“Warm ice melts. It is still water.”

Real world

Michigan snow

snowy yard melting.

“Snow is solid water. When it warms, it becomes liquid water.”

Concept 3

Properties help us identify materials

We can identify materials by observing properties like hardness, magnetism, solubility, and texture.

Try it

Property sort

objects: paper clip, eraser, wood chip, plastic bead.

“Sort by hard/soft, magnetic/not magnetic, sinks/floats.”

Data

Property table

table with columns: Object, Magnetic?, Sinks?, Dissolves?

“Properties are clues.”

Real world

Recycling

bins with paper, metal, plastic.

“Recycling uses properties to sort materials.”

Concept 4

Mixtures can be separated

A mixture keeps the properties of its parts, so we can often separate it.

Analogy

Trail mix

raisins, peanuts, cereal.

“You can pick trail mix apart. The pieces do not become one new thing.”

Try it

Sand and salt

cup with sand and salt, water, filter, spoon.

“Add water. Salt dissolves. Sand does not. Filter the sand.”

Data

Before/after table

drawings of mixture, filtered sand, salt water.

“The salt is still there, even when we cannot see it.”

Concept 5

Changes can be physical or chemical, but matter is conserved

Heating, cooling, mixing, and dissolving may change appearance, but total matter stays the same; some changes make new substances.

Diagram

Physical vs chemical

ice melting vs fizzing bag.

“Melting is still water. Fizzing can make a new gas.”

Try it

Sealed bag reaction

zip bag with vinegar and baking soda sealed inside.

“Mix inside the bag. The bag puffs with gas. If sealed, nothing escapes.”

Data

Balance stays level

simple hanger balance before and after mixing.

“The gas has mass. The total stays the same.”

Real world

Rust

rusty bike.

“Iron changes into rust. It is a new substance.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Design a method to separate a mixture of sand, salt, and small iron filings. Use a magnet for iron, water to dissolve salt, filtering for sand, then let the salty water dry on a dark plate so the salt comes back. Record steps and evidence. Criteria: separate all three materials. Constraints: one cup, one filter, one magnet, limited water.

Try it

What you need

zip bags, cups, spoons, salt, sugar, sand, coffee filters, rubber bands, small bags of baking soda and vinegar, two balloons, straw or hanger for balance, paper clips, small magnet, paper towels.

Safety: wash hands after sand/soil/salt work; adult handles warm water; keep magnets away from Chromebooks; keep iron filings in a closed bag and hands away from eyes; use a spoonful of baking soda and a splash of vinegar so the sealed bag puffs without popping; seal it over a tray and look away from the bag while it fizzes. An open bag lets gas escape, so its mass drops: that is a leak, not proof that gas weighs nothing.

Try it

What you do

Mix and separate sand/salt; observe dissolving; test air takes space; do sealed baking soda-vinegar bag and compare balance before/after. You did this before / what is new: You sorted materials in 2-A; in 5.1 you use property tests to identify unknowns and record a data table. You did this before / what is new: You used fair-test habits in Unit 0; here you use repeated measurements and graphs to show matter is conserved.

What did you learn?

Words to know

matter
anything that has mass and takes space.
particle
a tiny piece of matter.
solid
matter with a fixed shape.
liquid
matter that flows and takes the shape of its container.
gas
matter that spreads out to fill space.
mixture
two or more substances mixed but not chemically joined.
solution
a mixture where one substance dissolves.
property
a clue like color, hardness, or magnetism.
dissolve
when a substance breaks into tiny pieces in a liquid.
conserve
to stay the same total amount.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, standards, pacing

Pacing: five 30-minute sessions.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Air is nothing.” Correct: air is matter; it has mass and takes space.
  • “Only things you can see are matter.” Correct: matter includes things you cannot see, like air.
  • “Dissolved stuff disappears.” Correct: it is still there as tiny particles.
  • “Dissolved stuff becomes air or water.” Correct: it remains as the same substance, mixed in tiny pieces.
  • “Dissolving makes a new substance.” Correct: dissolving is a mixture; the substances stay themselves.
  • “Particles get bigger when heated.” Correct: particles move more; the substance may expand.
  • “Melting makes a new substance.” Correct: melting is a physical change; it is still the same substance.
  • “Gas has no weight.” Correct: gas has mass.

Limits and cautions:

  • Without a good balance, conservation of mass is harder to show. A homemade hanger balance helps but is less precise; the provided dataset guarantees the graphing evidence.
  • Chemical reactions are simplified: students observe signs of change but do not identify all products.
  • This unit does not cover temperature scales or detailed heat transfer; those belong in later energy units.
  • If magnets are used, keep them away from Chromebooks and cards.

Michigan Science Standards this unit earns:

  • 5-PS1-1: Develop a model that matter is made of particles too small to see.
  • 5-PS1-2: Measure and graph quantities to show that total weight is conserved during heating, cooling, or mixing.
  • 5-PS1-3: Identify materials by properties.
  • 5-PS1-4: Investigate whether mixing substances makes new substances.

Connections: Builds on: K–5 Unit 0: How Science Works; 2-A Materials and Their Uses. Builds toward: 5.3 Energy and Matter in Ecosystems; Unit 2 Thermal Energy; Unit 10 States of Matter; 7.1 Structure & Properties of Matter; 7.2 Chemical Reactions & Matter.
